content:
The ASVO 2026 Awards for Excellence winners. Image supplied

Last night, the Australian Society of Viticulture and Oenology (ASVO) revealed the winners of its Awards for Excellence.

The ASVO said the winners were chosen from a very high calibre and diverse range of submissions showing expertise across winemaking, viticulture and wine science.

Highlights of the evening included the naming of the 2026 ‘Viticulturist of the Year’ and 2026 ‘Winemaker of the Year’. In addition, the ‘Wine Science and Technology Award’, ‘Emerging Talent Award’, as well as the best Oenology and Viticulture research papers of the year were also announced.

 

Viticulturist of the Year sponsored by Syngenta

Chris Dent, ASVO 2026 Viticulturist of the Year. Image credit Kim Dent.

Chris Dent, owner of Gorton Drive Estate vineyard and chair of Murray Valley Winegrowers, was announced as the ASVO 2026 Viticulturist of the Year.

The panel highlighted his “unique contribution as both a working viticulturist and a strong advocate for inland growers, particularly during a period of major structural challenges for the region”.

Dent said he is “a bit floored” by the news of winning the title.

“Having your peers put your name up for this award is humbling enough — I can name plenty of others I’d rate above me. What I’m really chuffed about is what it says for the inland regions. We grow most of this country’s wine out here, through the hardest period a lot of us have seen — for this award to go to the Murray Valley in a year like this is genuinely appreciated — recognition for a corner of the industry that is easy to forget. That’s the real win, not me.

“None of it happens on your own, either — the networks and people you learn from along the way, through programs like Future Leaders, shape the way you farm and think. I owe a lot to those. Everything I do comes back to looking after the soil, farming sustainably, and letting the data tell me what’s going on. If there’s any advice in it — look after your dirt, farm with the future in mind, and build something that can get through the lean years.”

As chair of Murray Valley Winegrowers Incorporated and president of Swan Hill Wine Region Grape Growers Association, Dent has provided trusted industry leadership, representation and support for regional growers across the Murray Darling and Swan Hill regions.

He has strong credentials in sustainability, applies a regenerative approach to farming and adopts technology readily. He has demonstrated a more resilient model for warm-climate viticulture at his second-generation family-owned vineyards near Swan Hill by implementing soil-focused, climate-adaptive practices. He also hosts vineyard trials and demonstrations, including cover crop research in collaboration with the Australian Wine Research Institute, thus allowing other growers to learn from practical outcomes.

 

Winemaker of the Year sponsored by Tango Six

David Bicknell, ASVO 2026 Winemaker of the Year. Image credit Ovis Creative.

The ASVO’s 2026 Winemaker of the Year is David Bicknell — “an exceptional Australian winemaker whose influence extends well beyond his almost quarter of a century at Oakridge Wines”. His approach to winemaking “reflects a strong commitment to site expression, precision, balance and longevity, which helped redefine expectations of what Australian cool-climate wines could achieve”.

The judging panel found Bicknell a highly deserving recipient. They said his combination of technical excellence, sustained pursuit of quality, industry leadership, contribution to Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, commitment to the wine show system, and influence on other winemakers represents a significant contribution to Australian wine.

“I am humbled by this award from my peers — I came to wine as an outsider. Roseworthy (now Adelaide University) gave me the foundations, and from there into the industry I found a place full of clever, highly-skilled and imaginative people who mentored me and infected me with their passion,” Bicknell said.

“I found my people — friends and family. It’s my responsibility — and all of us — to share our accumulated knowledge and skills and I encourage the next generation of winemakers to never stop imagining how we can always do better.”

The ASVO said his win continues the legacy of Oakridge as a source of industry greatness, following Steve Faulkner being named Viticulturist of the Year last year.

 

Wine Science & Technology Award sponsored by WineChek

Tracey Siebert, recipient of the ASVO 2026 Wine Science and Technology Award. Image supplied.

The ASVO 2026 Wine Science and Technology Award was presented to Tracey Siebert.

Siebert was recognised for her “exceptional and sustained contribution to Australian wine science throughout her career, particularly her internationally recognised leadership in flavour chemistry and aroma research”. She is the AWRI’s most highly cited flavour scientist with around 2,800 citations across 48 indexed publications, and her papers have propelled the Australian wine industry to the forefront of flavour chemistry. Moreover, Siebert has given winemakers the tools to modulate wine aroma in a range of important areas — including black pepper, fermentation esters, stone fruit characters and struck flint aromas.

“It is an absolute honour to receive this award!” exclaimed Siebert.

“More than 25 years at the AWRI working with my fabulous flavour team but also in many projects across the organisation, with other colleagues on Waite campus, other research organisations in Australia and overseas, plus of course, our very helpful industry collaborators — I give my heartfelt thanks to them all, because without them, this would not have been possible.

“Along the way, I have had the pleasure of sharing my knowledge and experience while training, guiding, and supervising numerous local and international students, visiting scientists, as well as new staff. I love their enthusiasm to learn and then watching them apply those new skills and move ahead with their careers.”

 

Emerging Talent Award sponsored by Wine Network Consulting

From a large pool of “17 excellent submissions”, the 2026 Emerging Talent Award goes to Sarah Lavelle, direct-to-consumer & marketing manager at Seven Hill Cellars in Clare Valley.

Lavelle’s selection “reflected her strategic leadership and commitment to building capability across the Australian wine sector”. Through examples such as her contribution as the Rootlings State Champion for South Australia, SA Rural Ambassador of the Year and the development of the Wine Show Observer Program, she has “demonstrated an ability to identify industry needs and translate them into practical opportunities for emerging professionals”. The judges applauded her governance-focused leadership and strong national influence.

ASVO president Sam Scarratt said the organisation was delighted with the high number of quality submissions to the award, which is only its second year.

“Sarah Lavelle in an impressive young wine professional and was an excellent choice by the judges, but the choice was hard — the depth and breadth of the talent in the young people in our industry is stunning and it is uplifting to see so many be nominated,” Scarratt said.

 

Research papers

2026 Oenology Paper of the Year recipient Marina Serantoni. Image supplied.

The 2026 Oenology Paper of the Year was awarded to Marina Serantoni for her article on ‘Titanium-dioxide-Coated Glass Spheres as an Advanced Material for Wine Protein Stabilisation’, which judges said has the potential to provide a future alternative to bentonite. The paper “reflected her lifetime of accumulated expertise on materials surface science and supported the filing of a patent by the University of Bologna, Italy”.

2026 Viticulture Paper of the Year recipient Christine Böttcher. Image supplied.

The 2026 Viticulture Paper of the Year was authored by Christine Böttcher on the topic of ‘Efficient DNA-Free Protoplast Gene Editing of Elite Winegrape Cultivars for the Generation of Clones with Reduced Downy Mildew Susceptibility’. The judging panel considered the paper to “represent an outstanding combination of scientific excellence, innovation, relevance to Australian viticulture and potential long-term industry impact”.

Both research papers were published in the Australian Journal of Grape and Wine Research during 2025-2026.

title: Wine strives for sustainability; right now, AI is anything but
summary:
The Australian and New Zealand wine sector prides itself on sustainability. The very concept has become the industry’s bread and butter, quite frankly. Look at any winery website and you’ll find a dedicated page filled with paragraphs detailing all the initiatives reducing carbon emissions, saving water and limiting energy use that they are incredibly proud of (and rightfully so). It’s arguably become an expectation from consumers that wine is made sustainably, and the industry has loved going green. From lightweight bottles to off-grid systems, the sector seems acutely aware of every little environmental consequence that could arise from the process of bottling and selling a wine. Yet, strangely enough, AI-generated content appears to have pulled the wool over the industry’s eyes. From posters advertising wine tastings to silly social media clips right down to the wine labels themselves, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly adopted by the wine industry as a tool next to no one thinks twice about using — and why would they? It’s free, easily accessible and gives you results in a few seconds. But what if the reality is that AI has the potential to shatter the clean and green reputation wine has built for itself? Suppose that the very consumers it so desperately desires to recruit in this all-time consumption low could be sent running for the hills at the sight of one too many fingers wrapped around a wine glass? Well, as journalist Kyra Trussell discovered, that could very well be the case.

content:
The Australian and New Zealand wine sector prides itself on sustainability.

The very concept has become the industry’s bread and butter, quite frankly. Look at any winery website and you’ll find a dedicated page filled with paragraphs detailing all the initiatives reducing carbon emissions, saving water and limiting energy use that they are incredibly proud of (and rightfully so). It’s arguably become an expectation from consumers that wine is made sustainably, and the industry has loved going green. From lightweight bottles to off-grid systems, the sector seems acutely aware of every little environmental consequence that could arise from the process of bottling and selling a wine. Yet, strangely enough, AI-generated content appears to have pulled the wool over the industry’s eyes. From posters advertising wine tastings to silly social media clips right down to the wine labels themselves, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly adopted by the wine industry as a tool next to no one thinks twice about using — and why would they? It’s free, easily accessible and gives you results in a few seconds. But what if the reality is that AI has the potential to shatter the clean and green reputation wine has built for itself? Suppose that the very consumers it so desperately desires to recruit in this all-time consumption low could be sent running for the hills at the sight of one too many fingers wrapped around a wine glass? Well, as journalist Kyra Trussell discovered, that could very well be the case.

 

The invisible environmental cost

The rabbit hole of finding out just how much AI impacts the environment can be a perplexing one. Navigating conflicting statistics across news stories, social media platforms and anecdotal accounts can make the truth can feel further out of reach than before you started searching. That is why every effort has been made to rely predominately on the findings of academic, peer-reviewed research that is free to access and published in recent years. This ensures that the information presented is relevant and as accurate as possible at the time of publication, with readers able to investigate the primary sources for themselves with no paywalls.

There are two stages of energy consumption for AI: the training of a language model and the ongoing use of that model, often referred to as ‘inference’. In simple terms, a language model is a computer program taught to understand and generate human language. Most well-known AI platforms, such as ChatGPT and Copilot, are built on Large Language Models (LLMs), which are trained on vast amounts of text and other data. OpenAI shared all the way back in 2018 that the computational power needed to train the leading AI models had doubled roughly every 3.5 months since 2012, outpacing Moore’s Law prediction that the density of transistors and computing power will increase by a factor of two approximately every two years1. This “high rate of growth in computational demand” indicates that mass AI adoption is happening “much faster than improvements in hardware efficiency have been made historically”, which consequently “creates many serious issues regarding energy use, carbon emissions and overall environmental sustainability”2.

 

The impacts of training LLMs and developing AI

Given that AI relies heavily on electricity, with most of the world’s electricity still being generated using traditional fuel sources such as coal and gas, “fluctuations in power sources would indirectly increase the level of carbon emissions and their impacts associated with running an AI system”2.

For instance, one study found that “training a single large natural language processing model generates around 300,000 kg of CO₂ emissions”2. According to the National Transport Commission, average carbon dioxide emissions for registered light vehicles in Australia in 2025 were 191 grams per kilometre, or approximately 2.3 kilograms for every litre of petrol consumed3. That means an average light passenger car would need to travel approximately 1.57 million kilometres or use around 130,435 litres of petrol to produce CO₂ emissions equivalent to the training of one individual LLM. Alternatively, this is the equivalent of approximately 105 cars each driving 15,000 kilometres over a year. Recent studies have revealed potentially larger footprints for more sophisticated models, estimating that “training advanced transformer models can emit between 25 and 450 tonnes (25,000 and 450,000 kilograms) of CO₂, depending on data centre efficiency and energy sourcing”2.

Moreover, as oil prices fluctuate rapidly, the money spent on oil increases and the world faces periods of fossil fuel market instability, an AI-driven surge in electricity demand could further inflate the carbon intensity of powering AI systems2. By 2030, global data centres are estimated to consume 945 terawatt-hours of electricity (with AI demand to account for 40%) — “nearly triple the combined annual energy use of Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nigeria”, which are collectively home to 650 million people⁴. Even training a single model like ChatGPT has been estimated to consume 1.287 gigawatt-hours of electricity, “comparable to the annual consumption of 120 US households”2.

Similarly, the “rapid development of AI technologies has led to a significant rise in electronic waste”2, also known as e-waste. According to Clean Up Australia, e-waste is “the fastest growing component of the municipal solid waste stream” in the country and includes discarded electronic devices and parts⁵. In 2025, the average Australian produced 20 kg of e-waste, compared to the global average of 7 kg per person⁵. Research in 2020 estimated that 53.6 million metric tonnes (53.6 billion kilograms) of electronic waste was generated worldwide, with only 17.4% being “officially collected and recycled”6. In 2022, that number rose to 62 million tonnes5. E-waste contains several toxic additives and hazardous substances such as “mercury, brominated flame retardants (BFR), and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), or hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs)”⁶. Ineffective disposal and recycling of e-waste can lead to “toxic waste pollution in landfills and incinerators, endangering ecosystems and human health”2. A United Nations University study predicted that AI infrastructure could generate up to 2.5 million tonnes of electronic waste each year by 2030, roughly the equivalent of discarding 250 Eiffel Towers annually⁴.

 

How the average person using AI can be harmful

When it comes to the everyday use of AI, one of the biggest impacts is on the Earth’s most precious resource: water.

A simplified explanation for how this occurs is that AI data centres use water for processor chip-cooling technology to avoid the system overheating when fulfilling AI prompt requests⁷. Similar technology is used in some high-end desktop computers, although data centres deploy it on a much larger scale. The Environmental and Energy Study Institute claims that large data centres can consume up to 5 million gallons (18.93 million litres) per day, equivalent to the water use of a town populated by 10,000 to 50,000 people⁷. The associated water footprint of data centres by 2030 is estimated to equal “9.3 trillion litres, or enough to meet the minimum annual domestic water needs of all 1.3 billion residents of Sub-Saharan Africa for a full year”⁴. Alarmingly, data centre developers are reportedly “increasingly tapping into surface and underground aquifers to cool their facilities”, even as drought reduces water availability⁷. United Nations University research claims that in Querétaro, Mexico, despite prolonged drought, “AI data centres in the region are drawing on limited water supplies for cooling and energy production, intensifying pressure on communities already facing water shortages”⁴. Back in May 2023, a similar story arose in Uruguay as plans for a data centre “raised concerns over prioritising industrial demand over human consumption” after “severe drought depleted freshwater reserves and rising salinity made tap water unsafe to drink”⁴. Only 3% of the Earth’s water is freshwater and only 0.5% of all water is accessible and safe for human consumption⁷.

Now that we’ve established how AI consumes water and uses electricity, lets breakdown how much everyday users are expending.

ChatGPT alone is estimated to process around 2.5 billion prompts per day, with daily user interactions consuming 80-90% of AI’s total energy consumption4. A typical ChatGPT-style text query is around “200 times more energy-intensive than text classification” such as spam filtering⁴. The energy required to generate a typical AI image is enough to power a 10-watt LED bulb for 17 minutes, meanwhile, the energy used to make a high-complexity AI video could power that same bulb for 42 hours⁴. At a conservative estimate of 0.42 Wh (watt-hours) per text prompt, Chat GPT’s annual energy consumption translates to roughly 383 GWh (gigawatt-hours) of electricity per year⁴. Offsetting the associated carbon emissions would require an estimated “2.6 million tree seedlings grown for 10 years, enough trees to cover a land area the size of Manhattan”⁴.

Moreover, search engines like Google have increased their power consumption by implementing AI. The average Google search was once estimated to use 0.3 Wh of electricity, equal to driving roughly 0.0003 miles (0.000482803 kilometres) in a car⁸, however, with the integration of the AI Overview function, that number is nowadays estimated at 0.24 Wh⁹. Vijay Gadepally, a research scientist at the MIT Lincoln lab, flagged this concern all the way back in 2023⁸.

Comparatively, the water footprint for generating a single image is approximately two tablespoons (29 millilitres), however, this number jumps to a whopping 4.1 litres for a complex video — which is nearly equivalent to the water needs of one person for two days⁴.

Of course, there are many other digital tools that consume power and water, such as streaming services, yet AI’s consumption is growing rapidly due its mass usage and accessibility. Anyone can open websites like ChatGPT or Gemini and start using an AI model without charge. Additionally, rapidly expanding data centres and model training are a point of difference for AI’s emissions and resource usage.

 

Scrutiny from Gen Z

Usually, the younger generation are the first to embrace and master new technologies — look no further than mobile phones and the internet — and, while AI has been widely adopted, it has certainly not been lovingly embraced by Gen Z. If the wine industry hopes to recruit the next generation of wine drinkers anytime soon, the research indicates that openly using AI is not the ideal way to go about it.

The Governance Institute of Australia’s 2025 Ethics Index revealed a “sharp generational divide in attitudes toward AI”, with Gen Z recording the “strongest negative swing toward corporate use of AI, dropping from a net positive of +8 in 2024 to -11”1⁰. Furthermore, the Ethics Index placed AI “alongside embryo experimentation as one of the most ethically difficult issues facing Australians”1⁰. It ranks as the third most pressing ethical challenge, directly behind cost of living and housing affordability, and jumped seven points in the past year1⁰. Similar results have been observed in the US, with negative emotions among Gen Z toward AI intensifying over the past year11. A survey by Walton Family Foundation, GSV Ventures and Gallup found that “anger about the technology has risen, while excitement and hopefulness have dropped”11. The research found that even daily users of AI, who generally would have positive views of AI, have not become more positive11. Overall anxiety regarding AI sat at a steady 42% whilst hopefulness fell nine points to 18% and anger increased by nine points to 31%11. Furthermore, Harvard reported that 65% of Gen Zers surveyed “suggested that AI discourages engaging with ideas and information in a deep or critical way”12.

 

Marketing disdain and distrust

A study of 1,000 respondents across the USA, the UK and Germany explored “what people know about AI in marketing and how they feel about AI in general and about its use in marketing” in 2024. Just 21 per cent of survey participants had trust in AI companies and only 20 per cent trusted AI itself13. Furthermore, an experiment was conducted within the study on AI disclosure in advertising, with participants divided into two groups and shown the same six advertisements. One group saw the ads labelled as ‘AI-generated’ while the other saw them specified as ‘human-generated’. The study revealed “a clear pattern” where “labelling an ad as AI-generated led to a more critical evaluation”13. The participants “tended to see these ads as less natural and less useful, even though the content was identical to the ads labelled as humanmade”, with engagement directly affected13. Respondents reportedly showed a negative attitude towards the ad and their “willingness to research or purchase the product decreased”13. This clearly shows that there is a real risk for wineries using AI to promote their wines or events as, even if not commissioning a graphic designer can save money, there is money from product sales and all-important brand trust to be lost.

Moreover, even advertising on a website that heavily relies on AI content can be damaging for wineries. A 2025 article from Forbes covered a Nielsen study that found 55 per cent of the 6,000 participants felt “uncomfortable on websites that rely heavily on AI-generated articles and stories”, with 48 per cent going on to say they “do not trust brands advertising on such sites”1⁴.

With all of this in mind, it is not hard to see why the term ‘AI slop’ has been coined to express contempt for AI-generated content. The phrase has become a part of everyday social media vocabulary and even earnt itself a detailed Wikipedia page entry from how widely it is used. Memes making fun of the generic style of AI-generated posters promoting local events have even gone viral across social media, using the same layout a generated flyer would in order to call out the apparent “disgustingly unoriginal” content.

One of the many popular memes mocking AI generated posters circulating on social media.

Additionally, users on TikTok have begun making short videos openly expressing that if a business uses AI, they won’t support it or will even go out of their way to shame it. A video by user @claricetudor on TikTok shows the creator placing stickers on AI posters in public with phrases such as “this AI poster is UGLY and we’re all laughing at you” and “go generate yourself a sense of taste” to the tune of over 1.4 million views1⁵. The comments on the video question why businesses feel the need to use AI after years without the technology, and some users even ask the creator to sell the stickers so they can recreate the actions seen in the video1⁵. Moreover, a video of a BBQ stall with AI-generated food imagery taken by user @lovoros_ with 1.2 million views expresses how the advertising “doesn’t even look like food anymore”, with one commentor asking, “why do they even need AI when they can just take a picture of their food?”1⁶.

 

Stealing past work and future jobs

The earlier study on Gen Z’s perception of AI contained another interesting finding, that “employed Gen Zers are more than three times as likely to say the risks of AI in the workforce outweigh the potential benefits than to say the reverse”11. This statistic “reflects a more negative outlook than a year ago, when 37 per cent saw greater risks and 20 per cent greater benefits”11.

This is likely linked to AI beginning to replace humans in certain positions within the workplace. For example, as reported by Bloomberg, AI is already replacing humans in customer service roles at big corporations such as the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Microsoft Corp and Uber1⁷. The BBC even interviewed a 22-year-old artist, Aisha Belarbi, who had to stop replying on commissions as her main source of income because, in her words, “people can just generate whatever they want”1⁸. In 2024, Forbes covered the social media backlash Coca Cola received for AI-generating “deeply uncanny” Christmas video ads instead of hiring animators1⁹. Additionally, the UN University investigation found that “78% of organisations reported using AI in their work in 2024, and 40% of employers expect to reduce their workforce where AI can automate tasks”⁴.

So, AI is already beginning to do the work that humans would normally be paid to do — but the real kicker is, it’s actually humans who (often) unwillingly or unknowingly taught it how to do their jobs.

It was mentioned earlier in this article that the Large Language Models used to train AI are fed massive amounts of data. Turns out, this data often includes the hard work of artists, graphic designers, musicians and even journalists.

The Conversation reported this year that music from Kylie Minogue, John Farnham, INXS, Midnight Oil, AC/DC, Tones and I, Gotye, Ben Frost, Nick Cave, Tame Impala, Parkway Drive, The Living End and Vance Joy was found in a database of 12 million songs used to train AI on how to recognise and create music2⁰. Bestselling novelist David Baldacci testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2025 on how he believed his entire body of work had been used to train LLMs21. Sir Paul McCartney of The Beatles has even spoken out about this issue before, saying, “AI is a great thing, but it shouldn’t rip creative people off. Protect the creative thinkers, the creative artists, or you’re not going to have them. As simple as that.”21 The Copyright Alliance detailed how over 400 Hollywood professionals, including actors Mark Ruffalo and Ben Stiller, sent an open letter to the White House expressing concern over AI’s impact on the entertainment industry and calling for copyright protections21.

Furthermore, work that is published by authors without paywalls is easy for AI to access and consume. Theoretically, this can potentially lead to the content being paraphrased or summarised and presented as original content. Certain AI platforms even offer services to ‘humanise’ AI-generated text to help evade identification via AI detector tools.

This is precisely what one of Grapegrower & Winemaker’s own contributing writers, Edward Cavanagh, believes happened to him earlier this year.

Reading an article in an Australian metropolitan newspaper, Cavanagh explained that he “detected similarities in tone, terminology and logic” to one of his own paywall-free research articles covering the wine industry.

“‘While I suspect that this material was generated by an AI bot unwittingly for the author without him ever reading my article, this is difficult to prove; it is also mildly possible that the author clumsily summarised my article and reproduced it without attribution.”

He ran the text through several tools for article comparison, from AI detection to plagiarism, and the results were mixed. Still, Cavanagh said he cannot accept that it was a coincidence.

“Upon sharing my story with fellow wine writers on Substack and other online mediums, I’ve learned that experiences like this are becoming scarily common.

“It may be that all of this country’s wine writing — whether it takes the form of tasting notes, technical winemaking and viticultural notes, historical studies, policy analyses, or anything else — is going to be up for grabs,” he said.

Knowing that AI is trained on years of work from some of the most talented people on the planet both in and out of the wine industry without consent or compensation makes it unsurprising that anger towards the technology has increased year-on-year.

 

Closing thoughts

Between the massive environmental and moral implications of using AI, it may be in the best interest of wineries to avoid using the technology until such time as it better managed to avoid risking further loss of wine sales, damaging customer trust, turning new customers away and undoing the good of sustainability initiatives that the industry has worked years to achieve. Behind every generated image and chat bot prompt are tangible, real-world materials and theoretically measurable consequences for our ecosystems, communities and global climate goals⁴.

Hopefully, the time for a more sustainable and morally-just AI will come sooner rather than later for Australia, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announcing last month that the government is moving to “establish a set of Australian Standards for AI” and, significantly, promising that:

“Australian writers, musicians, artists and journalists must retain ownership and control of their work. Our laws will spell that out, plain as day…no company should use Australian books, music, art or news to build or train AI without the artist’s control.

“We will create a legal obligation for the next generation of large-scale data centres to underwrite new power supply. To pay their full share of grid connection, so no costs are passed on to homes or businesses. And to put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it. To be net-generators, not net-users.”22

The laws cannot come quickly enough, considering the sprinter’s pace AI has set.

summary:

The post Three-year partnership between Wine Australia and Wine Victoria to strengthen state’s wine sector appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
A new partnership between Wine Australia and Wine Victoria set to “fund a range of projects across the Victorian wine industry supporting grapegrowers and winemakers” has been announced today.

The two organisations are partnering over three years to fund projects that assist with the delivery of the Victorian Wine Strategy 2025–2030 and align with the One Grape & Wine Sector Plan.

The projects aim to strengthen sustainability, biosecurity preparedness, data-driven decision making and export capability. They intend to deliver practical support for Victorian wine businesses through field days, workshops, grower demonstrations, webinars, digital resources, benchmarking tools, sustainability and biosecurity education, and market-focused consumer insights “that can be applied directly to business and export decisions”.

The program combines $540,000 in Victorian Government funding secured by Wine Victoria with $346,667 in co-investment from Wine Australia through its Australian Wine Future Fund (AWFF) to “expand industry extension, knowledge translation, adoption and capability-building activities across the state”.

Wine Australia CEO Dr Martin Cole said the partnership would deliver practical, effective and data-driven information and insights for Victorian wine businesses.

“This partnership demonstrates the value of industry collaboration in translating research, technical expertise and market intelligence into practical outcomes for wine businesses,” he said.

“By working alongside Wine Victoria, we can amplify the reach and impact of existing investments, helping Victorian producers adopt sustainable practices, strengthen biosecurity preparedness, make better-informed business decisions and access valuable consumer insights from key export markets.”

Wine Victoria CEO Stephanie Duboudin said the partnership will help accelerate delivery of the Victorian Wine Strategy and provide producers with access to practical resources that address some of the industry’s most significant challenges and opportunities.

“Victorian wine businesses continue to operate in a rapidly changing environment, with increasing expectations around sustainability, biosecurity, business performance and market competitiveness,” she said.

“This partnership with Wine Australia allows us to build on existing investments and provide industry with practical support, trusted information and accessible tools that help businesses make informed decisions.”

The initiative will focus on four key areas:

  • Sustainable Winegrowing: Support for Victorian wine businesses to improve sustainability.
  • Biosecurity and Industry Preparedness: Building biosecurity awareness and supporting wine businesses to be prepared for risks.
  • Data and Better Business Decisions: Supporting effective financial and business decision-making through practical information and insights.
  • Export Consumer Insights: Translation of consumer findings into practical insights that support Victorian wineries’ export decision-making and capability.

The organisations explained that the partnership leverages Wine Australia’s Research & Innovation Fund (RIF), part of the AWFF, to attract co-investment for co-designed projects that deliver practical outcomes for vineyard performance, product innovation, sustainability and production efficiency.

AWFF is expected to achieve “an investment of $50 million for the Australian grape and wine sector over the next five years through a mix of Commonwealth matching, federal and state government grants, and partner investments”. It is aimed at “unlocking funding, creating additional value, accelerating investments and delivering impactful solutions for the wine sector”.

AWFF has two complementary streams:

Research & Innovation Fund: A target of $35 million over five years through external grants and partner co-investment, funding co‑designed projects that deliver practical outcomes for vineyard performance, product innovation, sustainability and production efficiency.

Venture Investments Portfolio: A target of $15 million over five years through attracting private capital that will be strategically invested to address critical innovation gaps.

content:
Anna Kelland, the 2026 Young Horticulturist of the Year. Image supplied

Marlborough viticulture technician Anna Kelland has won the Young Horticulturist of the Year title, having “excelled” in an intensive two-day competition in Auckland from 4-5 November.

Kelland was the 2025 New Zealand Young Viticulturist of the Year and therefore went through to represent the viticulture sector in this year’s Young Horticulturist competition.

The winner was only seven when she declared she wanted to be a winemaker when she grew up.

“When they didn’t have a core science competency session in the New Zealand curriculum, I got some intermediate level books at primary school and started learning for myself,” Kelland said.

She won a scholarship from Constellation Brands and now works for the company in Marlborough as a viticulture technician.

Kelland competed against four other future leaders in horticulture representing the grower, arborist, amenity and plant producer sectors. Over the two days, organisers said they faced a wide range of practical, technical, business and sustainability challenges as well as submitted an innovation project.

In addition to being the overall winner, she also won the Woolworths Innovation Project Award, the Woolworths Industry Knowledge Award and the Horticentre Charitable Trust Sustainability Award. Her prizes include a professional development scholarship, a glass trophy and cash totalling more than $25,000.

“Every day when I leave work, I look down our long driveway towards the stunning Richmond Ranges. That view reminds me of the impact provenance has on our industry,” she said.

“Our unique mix of soils and climates contribute to our biodiversity and the identity our produce has. Taking care of the land and being kaitiaki is of utmost importance if we want to keep growing and keep sharing that provenance with the world.”

Anna Kelland is the tenth Young Viticulturist to become Young Horticulturist of the Year, the others being Marcus Wickham, Emma Taylor, Caine Thompson, Stuart Dudley, Braden Crosby, Caleb Dennis, Annabel Bulk, Simon Gourley, and Rhys Hall.

Shaun Trevan, chair of the Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture Education Trust, says the competition was the closest it had been in several years.

“The competition identifies and celebrates high-potential young professionals who are contributing to the future of horticulture and provides mechanisms to continue to develop their skills and knowledge and provide opportunities to broaden their networks,” Trevan said.

“The Ministry for Primary Industries forecasts the sector — which employs approximately 60,000 people — is likely to reach $9.7 million in revenue next year, so horticulture is incredibly important to New Zealand. It is imperative we celebrate up-and-coming talent and nurture it.”

Second place was won by Phoebe Scherer. The Young Grower of the Year from the Bay of Plenty is an award-winning kiwifruit grower at Prospa by EastPack. She won more than $12,500 in prizes.

summary:

ANZ found that 41% of Australians are drinking less than a year ago or have stopped altogether, while only 6% are drinking more. Notably, “wine becomes more prominent through middle age, reaching 71% among 35–44s and 63% among 45–54s”. However, among 18–24-year-olds, beer reaches 64% and RTDs 46%, while spirits reach 68% among 25–34s. Additionally, the report emphasises that Australia’s liquor market is shifting from volume to value, with shoppers spending more per bottle-shop visit even as alcohol consumption moderates.

The post Wine remains Australia’s most purchased category as alcohol consumption moderates appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
New research shows that wine endures as “the most widely purchased category” in Australia at 55%, followed by spirits at 46% and beer at 44%.

The new ‘What’s Driving Australia’s Alcohol Shopper: Consumption, Channels, Promotions and Occasions’ report from Vypr and Shop! ANZ found that 41% of Australians are drinking less than a year ago or have stopped altogether, while only 6% are drinking more.

Notably, “wine becomes more prominent through middle age, reaching 71% among 35–44s and 63% among 45–54s”.

However, among 18–24-year-olds, beer reaches 64% and RTDs 46%, while spirits reach 68% among 25–34s.

Additionally, the report emphasises that Australia’s liquor market is shifting from volume to value, with shoppers spending more per bottle-shop visit even as alcohol consumption moderates.

48% now typically spend more than $40 per liquor-store shop, up from around 23% a year ago. Among 25–34-year-olds, 64% typically spend above $40.

“With many Australians continuing to cut back on alcohol, brands and retailers will need to compete harder for a share of spending on the occasions when people do choose to drink,” said Sam Gilding, chief revenue officer at Vypr.

“That means understanding who the shopper is, where they want to buy and what combination of product, format and price makes that purchase feel worthwhile.”

A few key findings from the report are as follows:

‘Category strategies need to become more targeted’

The report claims that the differences in wine purchase popularity across age groups points to “a need for more targeted ranging, channel and activation strategies rather than a single approach to all shoppers”.

It emphasises that the holiday season creates another growth opportunity, with Christmas Day influencing alcohol purchases for 52% of consumers, while Christmas parties and gifting influence 47% each and New Year’s Eve 46%.

Gilding added that it’s vital for brands and retailers to understand who they’re targeting and reflect those preferences in their range and promotions.

“Those differences matter as we head into Christmas. Someone buying a gift may be looking for something quite different from someone choosing drinks for a party. Helping shoppers find the right option for their occasion and budget will be important in winning that purchase.”

‘Younger shoppers are reshaping the path to purchase’

Physical retail “remains dominant, with 74% primarily buying alcohol in-store, but younger shoppers are increasingly omnichannel”.

Only 55% of 18–24-year-olds and 58% of 25–34-year-olds primarily shop in-store, while 37% of 25–34s combine physical and online purchasing. The findings suggest digital shopping is complementing rather than replacing physical retail, increasing the need for consistent ranging, pricing and promotion across channels.

‘Price still wins attention, but value is broadening’

Price remains the strongest influence at the point of purchase. Special price tickets are noticed by 63% of shoppers and influence product choice for 61%.

Loyalty points now influence 44% of shoppers, up from 28% for loyalty or member offers a year ago, while bonus packs influence 36% and cashback 33%.

“Price remains incredibly effective at stopping the shopper, but value is becoming broader than on-sale prices alone,” said Carla Bridge, general manager at Shop! ANZ.

“Loyalty, added product, sampling and staff advocacy on a product can all help move the consumer into purchase. The strongest activations will give shoppers a reason to stop and try.”

summary:

content:
Top row LTR: Jodie Armstrong and Luke Willis. Bottom row LTR: Nicole Brasier and Susi Whiting. Images supplied

Four South Australian wine industry representatives have been selected to travel to some of the world’s most renowned wine regions to “connect with international experts and explore new ideas and innovations”.

The South Australian Government explained that ‘The Great Wine Capitals Outbound Knowledge Exchange Bursary Program’ enables wine industry professionals, academics and researchers to visit world-renowned wine regions within the Great Wine Capitals Global Network, exchange knowledge with international peers and bring valuable insights back to South Australia.

The 2026–27 Outbound Knowledge Exchange Bursary Program recipients are:

  • Jodie Armstrong — McLaren Vale Grape Wine and Tourism Association, McLaren Vale (to visit Valparaiso-Casablanca Valley, Chile)
  • Nicole Brasier — Bleasdale Vineyards, Langhorne Creek (to visit Porto, Portugal)
  • Susi Whiting — Adelaide University, Adelaide (to visit Verona, Italy)
  • Luke Willis — Two Hands Wines, Barossa Valley (to visit Mendoza, Argentina)

Jodie Armstrong will explore how to use regenerative soil health practices, along with water and climate knowledge, to build healthier, more resilient vineyards.

Nicole Brasier will explore how the historic fortified wine region has adapted to change while maintaining its traditions in a modern industry, remaining relevant and appealing to premium visitors.

Susi Whiting will learn how vineyards are being used for practical teaching, research and industry engagement, including the region’s approaches to sustainability and adapting to climate change.

Luke Willis will explore how the region uses environmental sustainability practices and vineyard biodiversity to attract high-value international visitors and turn them into long-term direct-to-consumer customers and advocates.

The state government said the program offers valuable professional development opportunities that strengthen skills, encourage knowledge exchange and enable insights to benefit the state’s wine sector and support its resilience.

“South Australia is home to many of the world’s very best premium wine regions, so it’s important to stay ahead of the game by investing in the professionals who keep our state’s wine sector in the global spotlight,” said Clare Scriven, Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development.

“From sustainability and climate adaptation, to enhancing consumer experiences and engagement, each bursary recipient will explore practical innovations that can help to strengthen resilience and competitiveness in our wine sector.

“I congratulate Jodie, Nicole, Susi and Luke on being selected for bursaries through this program and I look forward to seeing how their experiences benefit the South Australian wine industry.”

Each bursary is valued at $6,000, supporting travel to one or more Great Wine Capitals between October 2026 and March 2027. During their travels, recipients will engage with academic, regional and industry experts, exchanging insights and gaining knowledge about global practices, sustainability and innovation in viticulture, winemaking, tourism and research.

Wine Grape Council of South Australia (WGCSA) CEO Lisa Bennier said the organisation is pleased to support a bursary and the opportunities it will provide for professional development.

“Supporting initiatives that build capability and encourage people to bring new knowledge and perspectives back to our industry is an important investment in its future,” Bennier said.

Australian Wine Industry Technical Conference chair Mark Krstic said they are excited to support Jodie Armstrong’s selection for a bursary.

content:

Levantine Hill is expanding into the US, marking a “major milestone” for the family-owned Yarra Valley estate.

Ranked number two in The Real Review’s Top Wineries of Australia 2026, the winery made its USA debut as the official wine partner of the American Australian Association’s 2026 New York Benefit Dinner.

On Thursday 5 November, the estate’s wines “were served to hundreds of leaders from business, government and diplomacy at the Manhattan gala, which counted many Fortune 500 companies among its sponsors”.

The winery explained that each guest was given a take home bottle of Levantine Hill’s 2019 Samantha’s Paddock Mélange Traditionnel, its flagship Cabernet blend.

“Levantine Hill was founded on the belief that Australian wines can stand alongside the finest in the world,” said chief winemaker Paul Bridgeman.

“Now we have an opportunity to bring that belief to the table in New York. We want American wine lovers to taste the character of our Yarra Valley vineyards and discover just how compelling cool climate Australian fine wine can be.”

Back in the Yarra Valley, the Jreissati family is preparing to open a 33-suite luxury hotel at Levantine Hill.

“We want someone to discover Levantine Hill over a glass of wine in New York, Las Vegas, Singapore or Seoul, then come to the Yarra Valley and experience the place it comes from,” said marketing director Melissa Jreissati.

“Bringing our wines to the United States builds on Levantine Hill’s ambition to be an international beacon for Australian fine wine and bring our wines to more tables around the world. When our Yarra Valley hotel opens, we’ll be able to welcome more international guests to our very own Yarra Valley table.”

The post Charlotte Newton awarded Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Charlotte Newton has been awarded the Dux prize for 2026. Image supplied

Charlotte Newton, owner and winemaker at Cha Cha Wines in Western Australia, has been awarded the Basil Sellers Prize for Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial.

Newton, along with 11 other Australian wine professionals, took part in the 24th Tutorial held at Spicer’s Guesthouse in the Hunter Valley from 2 to 6 November. As Dux, Charlotte receives $10,000 to further her global wine education.

Originally from New Zealand, Newton studied winemaking at Christchurch’s Lincoln University before building her career in Australia and overseas. Her 25-year career has spanned winemaking, viticulture, wine education and sensory evaluation, with 15 years as a WSET educator.

“I am incredibly proud and honoured to have been awarded Dux of the 2026 Len Evans Tutorial,” Newton said.

“To have been accepted into the Tutorial was a privilege in itself, and the experience exceeded all expectations. I had the opportunity to taste some of the most exceptional wines of my life, form lasting friendships and learn alongside an inspiring group of wine professionals.

“I will cherish these memories for many years to come and look forward to continuing to share my passion for fine wine through wine education and winemaking. Finally, my sincere thanks to the late Len Evans for his vision and to his daughter Sally Evans for continuing his remarkable legacy.”

Selected from a record 193 applications, the 12 scholars represented some of Australia’s most promising wine talent, spanning winemakers, media and trade professionals. Over an intensive week, they learnt from an exceptional line-up of world-class tutors, gaining the knowledge, skills and experience to help shape the future of Australian wine. The programme aims to strengthen the next generation of wine professionals and wine show judges.

“As we see each year via the rigorous selection process, performance remained tight across the cohort for the majority of the week and Charlotte was not only consistent, [but] she [also] spoke to the wines with a deep conviction,” said Sarah Crowe, LET tutor and deputy chair.

“In the final few sessions, this year’s Dux did not falter and was the top performer in the written exercise as well as the final tasting of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti.”

The scholars undertook masterclasses from Australia and further afield, including Henschke, led by Prue and Stephen Henschke, Barolo and Barbaresco with the UK’s David Gleave MW, Burgundy, Prestige Champagne, Hunter Valley Semillon with a vertical of Tyrrell’s Vat 1 with Chris Tyrrell and concluding with Friday’s showcase of Domaine de la Romanee-Conti.

A core component of the programme is the five judging workshops, each featuring 30 wines served blind. These judging sessions focus on grape varieties and styles relevant to the Australian wine industry, this year covering Shiraz, Cabernet Sauvignon blends, Pinot Noir, Riesling and Chardonnay.

  • 2025 Yabby Lake Single Vineyard

The tradition of formal dinners continued each evening, starting with a deep dive into the ‘History and Heritage of Australia Wine’ lead by Andrew Caillard MW. A series of aged and rare wine flights were presented, “offering scholars a unique opportunity to experience exceptional vintages that may not be readily available elsewhere”.

“Another great year for the LET, with enthusiasm for the tutorial reaching record levels. Huge thanks to all who helped create a life-changing experience for our 2026 scholars. Whilst sharing, tasting and talking about wine quality is a key focus, the tutorial has also become a vital hub for sharing Australia’s rich wine history. My father achieved many things in his life, but the tutorial is perhaps his most meaningful legacy,” said chair Sally Evans.
